title: Balanced Search Tree From a Sorted List
statement:
You get an array nums of distinct integers in strictly increasing order. Build a binary search tree that holds every value exactly once and is height-balanced: at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Return its root.

Several trees usually qualify, and any valid one is accepted. The checker reads your tree back, confirms that an in-order walk gives exactly nums, and confirms the balance rule at every node.

Trees are shown in level order with null for missing children.

examples.why: The middle value 0 becomes the root, so each side gets two values. [0, -1, 8, -4, null, 3] is just as good.
Two values: either can be the root. [2, 1] is also accepted.
Making 1 the root and hanging the rest to the right gives a valid search tree, but it is a chain of height 7, not balanced.

hints: In a search tree, everything left of the root is smaller and everything right of it is bigger. Which value of a sorted list splits it most evenly?
Choose the middle value as the root. The values before it form the left subtree and the values after it form the right subtree.
Recurse on index ranges [lo, mid − 1] and [mid + 1, hi] instead of slicing arrays. An empty range returns null.

explain.intuition:
The sorted order is exactly the in-order walk of any search tree over these values, so the only real choice is which value sits at each root. Picking the middle value leaves equally many values on each side (or one more on one side). Doing the same for each half keeps every subtree as even as possible, so heights never differ by more than one.

It is divide and conquer, like building a balanced menu from a sorted list of options: split at the middle, then split each half.
steps: Define build(lo, hi) over the index range of nums.
Let mid = (lo + hi) >> 1 and create a node with nums[mid].
Set its left child to build(lo, mid − 1) and its right child to build(mid + 1, hi).
pitfalls: Inserting the values one by one in sorted order. Each new value goes to the far right, so the tree becomes a chain.
Slicing arrays in every call. It works, but copies O(n log n) values in total. Pass index bounds instead.
Off-by-one in the ranges: including mid again in a child range repeats a value or loops forever.

solutions.title: Middle value as root, recursively
solutions.idea: The middle of each index range becomes that subtree's root; the two halves become its children.

followups: The input is a sorted linked list instead of an array. How do you avoid finding the middle again in every call?
Given an existing unbalanced search tree, rebalance it in O(n) time.
lcTitle: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
